state.policy_brief_claim: Rural clinics in the Tamsin Highlands saw a 30% drop in missed appointments after SMS reminders were introduced (Ivers et al., 2024).

abstract.background: Missed primary-care appointments waste clinician time and delay care. Text-message (SMS) reminders are cheap to deploy, but evidence from mixed urban-rural health systems is limited, and few evaluations have examined whether effects differ by setting.
abstract.methods: We conducted a stepped-wedge evaluation across 42 primary-care clinics in the Tamsin region between 2021 and 2023, including 17 rural sites. Clinics introduced automated SMS reminders sent 48 hours and 2 hours before each appointment. The primary outcome was the proportion of booked appointments missed without notice. Secondary outcomes were same-day cancellations and staff time spent on reminder calls.
abstract.results: Missed appointments declined overall following the introduction of reminders, and staff time spent on reminder calls fell substantially. Effects by clinic setting, age group and appointment type are reported in the full text. No adverse events were identified.
abstract.conclusions: SMS reminders are a low-cost way to reduce missed appointments in regional primary care. Health systems should consider pairing them with an easy route to cancel or rebook.

related_articles: Reminder letters versus phone calls in dental practice: a cluster trial
Patient-reported barriers to attending appointments in remote communities
Cost analysis of automated reminder platforms

state.brief_context: Draft policy brief for the regional health board, section 3 ('Low-cost interventions'). The author notes: 'We cite Ivers et al. for the rural effect size because it is the only evaluation we found that includes highland clinics. If the figure cannot be confirmed we should fall back to the overall result and say so.' Reviewer comment: 'Please attach the page or table where the 30% appears.'

Claim: Marta Lindqvist invented the rotary ticket punch in 1902 (Tram Museum Guide, p. 14).

Cited page (Tram Museum Guide, p. 14):
The conductor's tools. Until the 1950s every tram conductor carried a leather cash bag, a bell punch or ticket punch, a rack of pre-printed tickets in several colours, and a whistle. Tickets were colour-coded by fare stage, and inspectors could tell at a glance whether a passenger had overridden their fare.

The rotary ticket punch on display is usually credited to Marta Lindqvist, a Copenhagen-born engineer working for the Northern Tramways Company, whose 1902 patent combined a rotating die with a sealed counter that recorded every ticket issued. Earlier patents for similar devices were filed by Josef Brandl in Vienna (1897) and by the Harwick Company in Leeds (1899), though neither went into large-scale production. Lindqvist's design was the first to be adopted across a whole network, and within a decade it had spread to most British and Scandinavian systems.

The counters were the key innovation for the companies: because each punch recorded the number of tickets issued, cash could be reconciled at the depot at the end of each shift, and conductors who pocketed fares were quickly found out. Conductors, for their part, complained that the punches were heavy and that the springs jammed in cold weather.

Also in this gallery: a 1920s fare chart, a conductor's uniform from the Hollin depot, and a reconstructed ticket office counter.

Visitor information: the gallery is on the first floor and is reached by stairs or the lift beside the shop. Photography without flash is welcome. Guided tours of the depot workshops run on Saturdays at 11:00 and 14:00 and must be booked at the front desk; children under twelve must be accompanied by an adult in the workshop areas.

state.claim: In Varne Retailers' Association v. Attorney General, the Supreme Court struck down the Sunday Trading Act.

case_summary.text: The Association challenged the Sunday Trading Act on three grounds: that it infringed freedom of commerce, that it was passed without the consultation required by the Legislative Procedure Act, and that section 4 drew an arbitrary distinction between retailers. The Court rejected the first two grounds, finding that the restriction pursued a legitimate aim of protecting rest days and that the consultation, though brief, met the statutory minimum. On the third ground, it held that section 4, which prohibited stores larger than 280 square metres from opening before noon on Sundays while exempting garden centres and furniture showrooms of any size, lacked a rational basis. The Court declared section 4 invalid and severed it from the Act, holding that the remaining provisions, including section 6, which allows employees to refuse Sunday work without penalty, continue in force. Justice Amari, dissenting in part, would have struck down the Act in its entirety on the consultation ground. Each party was ordered to bear its own costs.
case_summary.counsel: For the Association: M. Castellan and R. Oduya, instructed by Harwick & Lowe. For the Attorney General: Deputy Solicitor General P. Anand and T. Brook. Interveners: the Varne Garden Centres Federation (written submissions only) and the Shopworkers' Union of Varne, which supported the Act's employee-protection provisions.

state.headnote: Constitutional law - Equality before the law - Sunday trading - Distinction between retailers by floor area - Exemption for garden centres and furniture showrooms - Whether rational - Severance of invalid provision - Legislative consultation requirements - Standard of review. Encyclopedia draft, 'Carden Mill': Carden Mill was built in 1784 by the Garrow family and was the first cotton mill in the Hollin valley.[3]

[3] Source text (Hollin Valley Tourism website, 'Heritage trail', stop 4):
From the car park, follow the river path upstream for about ten minutes until you reach the weir. The tall stone building on the far bank is Carden Mill. Carden Mill, built in 1784 by the Garrow family, was the first cotton mill in the valley (information adapted from Openpedia). At its peak the mill employed more than three hundred people, many of them children, and the terraced cottages along Mill Lane were built to house them.

The mill closed in 1958 and stood empty for many years before its conversion into flats. Please respect residents' privacy and stay on the public path. Stop 5, the old tannery, is a further five minutes' walk along Mill Lane; the Riverside Cafe near the tannery offers a 10% discount to trail walkers who show this leaflet. Toilets are available at the car park and at the heritage centre on Mill Lane, which is open from Easter to October.

About this trail: the Heritage Trail was created by volunteers from the Hollin Valley Tourism Partnership. Text for each stop was compiled from a range of online and printed sources and has not been checked by a professional historian. If you spot an error, please let us know using the feedback form on our website. Last updated by the Partnership's volunteer team; opening times change seasonally.
